title: Cole Palmer, penalty master: The experts explain the secrets behind his prowess
content:
What makes Cole Palmer so good at penalties?

Asking the man himself does not get you very far. Many have tried, and many have failed.

“I don’t have one,” Palmer said when asked by the BBC’s Football Daily podcast about his approach to spot kicks before Euro 2024. “I’m actually not even joking, I don’t have an approach.”

Even his own mother didn’t have much luck. “What do you think goes through your mind when you take these penalties?” she asks him in a clip from Amazon Prime Video’s documentary The New Generation, released in 2025.

“What goes through my mind? Not much.”

“It must be something…”

“Yeah, obviously, I think, ‘Score’. What else am I gonna think?”

Palmer is one of the best penalty takers in Premier League history. His three conversions in the past two league games against Leeds United and Wolverhampton Wanderers mean he has scored 18 of 19 spot kicks in the competition.

He shares the record for the longest perfect streak, having scored his first 12 penalties before Leicester City’s Mads Hermansen saved one. Only Raul Jimenez has achieved the same, and only Jimenez, Matt Le Tissier, and Yaya Toure have a better conversion rate than Palmer’s 94.7 per cent among players who have taken at least 11 penalties.

Palmer is superb from the spot — but he either has an excellent poker face, or genuinely doesn’t think too hard about why that is.

Fortunately, plenty of others have pondered it. The Athletic spoke to experts in biomechanics, psychology, penalties, and goalkeeping to break down his success.

The story of Palmer as a penalty expert started early in his Chelsea career. His first four goals for the club came from the spot, which penalty expert Ben Lyttleton says has helped build a narrative about his expertise.

“A player who has great promise and has great talent and has great potential is now viewed as a penalty specialist,” Lyttleton says, “and that changes the narrative around every penalty that he will take after that.”

Any goalkeeper knows to expect Palmer to step up once a penalty is given, and is likely to have studied him well in advance. But Lyttleton, who wrote Twelve Yards: The Art and Psychology of the Perfect Penalty Kick, says that analysis only goes so far against the 23-year-old. Palmer mixes up his placement — he has never gone the same way more than three times in a row.

“What makes a really, really good penalty kick taker is when they have that variation,” says The Athletic’s goalkeeping expert Matt Pyzdrowski. “Some other takers don’t have that variation, or maybe they have a 60-40 (split) to one side versus the other — then, you can start to predict their strike. But with Palmer, that’s very, very difficult.”

Lyttleton explains that there are two ways to approach a penalty: goalkeeper-dependent, where the taker waits for the goalkeeper to make the first move before shooting the other way, and goalkeeper-independent, where the taker picks their spot and relies on power to beat the goalkeeper even if they guess correctly.

“Palmer’s technique seems to be more goalkeeper-independent,” Lyttleton says. “He’s not slowing down his run-up. He’s got a very fluid, quite fast run-up, and he’s not waiting for the goalkeeper to move before he picks his spot. But he is doing something to make the goalkeepers go the wrong way.”

In Palmer’s 19 penalties, he has sent the goalkeeper the wrong way 14 times.

“There’s something about that which makes me wonder if he’s doing something quite cool and unique,” Lyttleton says, “which is his run-up and approach points to goalkeeper-independent, but his actual choice of direction might be something to do with goalkeeper-dependent.”

Palmer has said that he occasionally changes his mind during his run-up, which Lyttleton explains is rare and generally “the worst thing you can do” — particularly for non-frequent penalty takers. But gradually breaking down Palmer’s technique illustrates how he can be so accurate, even with a last-minute change.

“One thing that caught my eye was the direction of the support foot,” says Archit Navandar, assistant professor of biomechanics at Madrid’s polytechnic university. “The way Palmer’s planted foot is pointing indicates which way he will shoot.

“Go frame by frame,” Navandar says, slowing down footage of Palmer’s first penalty against Wolverhampton Wanderers, “and see that he moves his foot outwards.

“That allows him to rotate his hip and then place the penalty on the other side.”

This ability to shift at the last minute, Navandar says, is a marker of an “elite” penalty taker — Harry Kane can also turn his ankle at the last moment in the same way.

Palmer’s approach is uncomplicated but lethal. “You look at Raul Jimenez or Bruno Fernandes who stutter-step in their approach and even hop at the end, so it can be very difficult for the goalkeeper to time their dive,” says Pyzdrowski. “The thing that’s interesting with Palmer is that he doesn’t do any of that.

“He’s very straightforward, but he’s so incredibly accurate and he hits the crap out of the ball.

“When he hits the ball as hard as he does, it’s very hard to make a save because you need time to throw yourself towards the ball, and he takes that away with his incredible strikes.”

Except for Hermansen’s save, the other goalkeepers who have correctly guessed the side Palmer chooses — Tottenham Hotspur’s Guglielmo Vicario, Manchester City’s Ederson, Liverpool’s Alisson, and Bournemouth’s Djordje Petrovic — still have reached them.

“He’s not like Cristiano Ronaldo, who has a lot of muscle mass on his thighs, that he’s able to transfer momentum from that,” Navandar says.

“If you see Lionel Messi taking a penalty, it’s about three steps or four steps and not running so fast as (Palmer) does, or even Kylian Mbappe. But those are strong players who get a lot of elastic energy in the cocking motion of the kick.

“With Palmer, it’s more about transferring momentum, more about power from the run up and then that he kicks the ball as hard as possible by striking at the centre of the ball.”

Palmer has a fairly long run-up and a large leg swing, and his stance allows him to transfer that momentum.

“Compare it to a golf swing or, or hitting a six in cricket,” Navandar continues. “You’ve got to hit it in such a way that the foot, the club or the bat is at a particular distance to hit the ball at the right time. The best way to do that is by placing the centre of the supporting foot in line with the centre of the ball.

“If you’re too close, you can’t transfer the power. If you’re too far, you might not be able to get the right transfer of momentum.”

Palmer also strikes the ball dead at its centre — which means it is struck on a flat trajectory, rather than generating any lift or spin. Navandar explains that keeping shots low also exploits goalkeepers’ technique: many take a first step forward before pushing off into their dive, which helps them cover more distance, but often means a ‘rainbow’ trajectory, which can delay them reaching the ball. The alternative is a straight dive, which is quicker, but harder to cover as much distance with.

“I don’t know if he understands this consciously or subconsciously,” Navandar says, “but he has to go in for the far corners. That is very difficult for the goalkeeper to reach in either of the techniques.”

Navandar also points out how Palmer uses his full upper body to generate extra power: “His back is not necessarily in a straight line. It’s sort of curved. He’s able to put his chest out and then extend his lower back and involve that as well in the hip extension.

“It’s like swinging with a stronger club, with an iron rather than a putter.”

Rather than trying to confuse goalkeepers with a complicated run-up, simplicity is Palmer’s secret.

“He relies on his instincts, and that’s part of what makes him a great player,” Lyttleton says. “He’s trusting his ability rather than overthinking it. And that can be a superpower when it comes to penalties.”

There is an obvious mental element to penalties, as sports psychologist Dan Abrahams explains.

“A combination of high importance and high expectations to succeed increases the volume of negative thoughts, emotions, feelings that place a greater amount of pressure on somebody,” Abrahams says.

“There’s a whole bunch of individual and contextual factors impinging on his mindset in that situation, one of which is that he’s been highly successful in the past.

“That can go one of two ways. That could be, ‘I’ve been highly successful, so subsequently I’m really confident I can do it again’, or ‘I’ve been highly successful in the past, well, I might miss one at one stage, I hope it’s not now’.”

The fact Palmer has scored four penalties since his return from injury, Abrahams says, hints at his confidence — as does his response to his only unsuccessful one.

“Sometimes if a player misses a penalty, they will go back to the drawing board and think, ‘What do I need to change?’.” Lyttleton adds. “Palmer has changed nothing. He’s almost doubled down on his technique.

“I spent two years studying penalties and speaking to every expert, and essentially, penalties are a duel of psychology more than anything else.

“All these players in the Premier League are amazing footballers, and they should all score all the time, but the ones who are really strong at penalties are the ones who are psychologically just so strong. We see that with Palmer.”

Eleven of Palmer’s spot kicks have either drawn Chelsea level or put them in front. That includes stoppage-time equalisers against Manchester United and Manchester City. He also opted for a late Panenka to seal Chelsea’s 4-3 win over Tottenham Hotspur in 2024, a game in which Chelsea had already come back from 2-0 down. His reasoning?

“The day before I said I was gonna chip and all the players were like, ‘Nah, you’re not going to’,” he told the BBC’s Football Daily.

“I told my mates that I was going to chip it if I got a penalty. And I told my dad, but my dad was thinking, ‘Shut up, man, you’re not’.

“When the penalty got given, I thought, ‘I’m going to have to chip it because I’ve told everyone I’m going to’. I thought I might as well try it, it is what it is, and then it went in.”

Palmer’s penalty success is built on inch-perfect placement, power — and his trademark approach of not taking anything too seriously.

“If there’s any doubt about whether he should have a place in the World Cup squad,” Lyttleton says, “his penalty prowess should definitely be factored in.”
